highlightAliases.old: Nutrition-Activity Interrelationship Nutrition and physical activity are closely linked, each having vitally important and interacting effects on body composition, functional ability, and well-being.
highlightAliases.new: Nutrition-Activity Interrelationship

highlightAliases.old: Nutrition-Disease Interrelationship There is a complex interrelationship between nutrition, health status, and clinical outcomes.
highlightAliases.new: Nutrition-Disease Interrelationship

highlightAliases.old: Changes in Body Composition With advancing age, there are significant changes in body composition that affect the nutritional needs of the individual.
highlightAliases.new: With advancing age, there are significant changes in body composition that affect the nutritional needs of the individual.

highlightAliases.old: Changes in Appetite and Energy Intake Regulation Maintenance of a stable weight requires a steady balance between nutrient intake and energy expenditure.
highlightAliases.new: Maintenance of a stable weight requires a steady balance between nutrient intake and energy expenditure.

highlightAliases.old: With advancing age, the metabolic, neural, and humoral pathways that normally maintain this delicate balance by regulating appetite and hunger begin to lose their compensatory
highlightAliases.new: With advancing age, the metabolic, neural, and humoral pathways that normally maintain this delicate balance by regulating appetite and hunger begin to lose their compensatory responsiveness to changes in energy demands.

highlightAliases.old: Pathophysiologic Changes that Lead to Loss of Taste, Smell, and Appetite with Advancing Age Numerous pathologic and age-related physiologic changes can have a deleterious effect on eating habits and the likelihood of maintaining an adequate diet (see Table 30-1).
highlightAliases.new: Pathophysiologic Changes that Lead to Loss of Taste, Smell, and Appetite with Advancing Age

highlightAliases.old: Psychological, Socioeconomic, and Cultural Influences on Appetite After the seventh decade of life, psychological, socioeconomic, and cultural factors are increasingly important for an adequate diet (see Table 30-1).
highlightAliases.new: Psychological, Socioeconomic, and Cultural Influences on Appetite

highlightAliases.old: For these reasons, the American Dietetic Association in collaboration
highlightAliases.new: For these reasons, the American Dietetic Association in collaboration with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, Pioneer Network, and others published a position statement suggesting that use of therapeutic diets in nursing homes be restricted.

highlightAliases.old: Definition and Prevalence Obesity is defined as an unhealthy accumulation of body fat, which leads to a higher risk of medical illness and premature death.
highlightAliases.new: Definition and Prevalence

highlightAliases.old: Potential Benefits and Adverse Consequences of Obesity There is controversy regarding the potential benefits and adverse consequences of being overweight or obese after age 65.
highlightAliases.new: Potential Benefits and Adverse Consequences of Obesity

highlightAliases.old: However, this does not necessarily indicate that older
highlightAliases.new: However, this does not necessarily indicate that older adults who have been slender all of their lives are at increased risk of mortality.

highlightAliases.old: Weight-Associated Morbidity The impact of obesity on overall health, functional status, and quality of life in older adults is more certain.
highlightAliases.new: Weight-Associated Morbidity

highlightAliases.old: The result is a lower functional reserve, chronic
highlightAliases.new: The result is a lower functional reserve, chronic pain, and an increased risk of disability.

highlightAliases.old: Interventions Targeting Obesity Given the increased risk of disability associated with obesity, controlled weight loss may be an appropriate therapeutic option for selected older adults.
highlightAliases.new: Interventions Targeting Obesity

highlightAliases.old: Components of a Weight Loss Program for Older Adults Upon committing to a weight loss program, an older adult should undergo a careful medical evaluation, which should include a detailed history and physical examination as well as a very careful assessment of the potential risks and benefits of both exercise and diet.
highlightAliases.new: Components of a Weight Loss Program for Older Adults

highlightAliases.old: Protein Because of the paucity of high-quality nutrition studies with adequate representation from older age groups, current recommendations for protein intake do not differentiate adults over the age of 65 from those who are younger.
highlightAliases.new: Because of the paucity of high-quality nutrition studies with adequate representation from older age groups, current recommendations for protein intake do not differentiate adults over the age of 65 from those who are younger.

highlightAliases.old: Factors That Influence the Protein Requirements of Older Individuals The protein requirements of an individual can change with time, being influenced by age, nonprotein content of the diet, activity level, medications, and health status.
highlightAliases.new: Factors That Influence the Protein Requirements of Older Individuals

highlightAliases.old: Carbohydrates Recommendations for carbohydrate content of the diet are generally based on two considerations, the source of the carbohydrates and the energy requirements of the individual.
highlightAliases.new: Recommendations for carbohydrate content of the diet are generally based on two considerations, the source of the carbohydrates and the energy requirements of the individual.

highlightAliases.old: Concentrated sources of dietary fiber may also be helpful in the treatment of chronic constipation when a limited variety of food is available or the amount of food consumed
highlightAliases.new: Concentrated sources of dietary fiber may also be helpful in the treatment of chronic constipation when a limited variety of food is available or the amount of food consumed is inadequate.

highlightAliases.old: Vitamin and Mineral Supplementation Many older adults, including those who are healthy and living independently as well as those who are frail, ill, or institutionalized, are at risk for micronutrient deficiencies.
highlightAliases.new: Vitamin and Mineral Supplementation

highlightAliases.old: Thus, older adults should be counseled not to exceed the tolerable ULs (see Table 30-5) for vitamin intake and to
highlightAliases.new: Thus, older adults should be counseled not to exceed the tolerable ULs (see Table 30-5) for vitamin intake and to disclose all vitamin and mineral supplement use whenever medications are reviewed by health professionals.

highlightAliases.old: These signs and symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency are nonspecific and common in many older adults
highlightAliases.new: These signs and symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency are nonspecific and common in many older adults with comorbid disorders.

highlightAliases.old: Calcium From adolescence onwards, both men and women should consume between 1000 and 1200 mg of elemental calcium daily, unless there are unique nutrition requirements.
highlightAliases.new: From adolescence onwards, both men and women should consume between 1000 and 1200 mg of elemental calcium daily, unless there are unique nutrition requirements.

highlightAliases.old: Nutrition, Cardiovascular Disease, and Cancer There is a growing body of evidence that nutrition plays an important role in CVD prevention.
highlightAliases.new: Nutrition, Cardiovascular Disease, and Cancer

highlightAliases.old: Nutrition and Age-Related Eye Diseases Evidence to support a protective effect of individual vitamin and mineral supplements on age-related eye diseases is conflicting.
highlightAliases.new: Nutrition and Age-Related Eye Diseases

highlightAliases.old: Initial Screening Assessment The risk of developing one or more nutritional disorders increases with age.
highlightAliases.new: Initial Screening Assessment

highlightAliases.old: A weight loss of 5% or more within the prior 3 months or 10% or more within the
highlightAliases.new: A weight loss of 5% or more within the prior 3 months or 10% or more within the prior 6 months to 3 years should be considered indicative of a potentially serious nutritional problem unless the weight fluctuation can be ascribed with certainty to alterations in fluid balance, such as those with heart failure or on hemodialysis.

highlightAliases.old: Assessment of Nutrient Intake Although frequently difficult to obtain, a detailed nutrient and caloric intake assessment is often the most critically needed part of the nutritional assessment.
highlightAliases.new: Assessment of Nutrient Intake

highlightAliases.old: Epidemiology Prevalence data, relying on a variety of measures of nutritional adequacy, suggest that deficiencies in macronutrients (protein energy) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) are very common among older adults.
highlightAliases.new: Prevalence data, relying on a variety of measures of nutritional adequacy, suggest that deficiencies in macronutrients (protein energy) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) are very common among older adults.

highlightAliases.old: A still greater reduction in caloric intake to levels that may be below daily requirements has been a consistent finding of nutritional surveys conducted among community-dwelling
highlightAliases.new: A still greater reduction in caloric intake to levels that may be below daily requirements has been a consistent finding of nutritional surveys conducted among community-dwelling older adults.

highlightAliases.old: Presentation and Evaluation Despite its clinical importance, malnutrition is often missed clinically.
highlightAliases.new: Presentation and Evaluation

highlightAliases.old: Assessment for Causes of Weight Loss Initial management of patients with PEM and/or weight loss should include a thorough evaluation to identify
highlightAliases.new: Assessment for Causes of Weight Loss

highlightAliases.old: While efforts to improve nutrition, even in patients with serious underlying disease, are often warranted, late in the course of disease
highlightAliases.new: While efforts to improve nutrition, even in patients with serious underlying disease, are often warranted, late in the course of disease appropriate palliative care may include, if not mandate, discontinuing such efforts.

highlightAliases.old: Enteral Nutrition Enteral nutrition (EN) is defined as the nonvolitional delivery of nutrients by tube into the GI tract.
highlightAliases.new: Enteral nutrition (EN) is defined as the nonvolitional delivery of nutrients by tube into the GI tract.

highlightAliases.old: Megestrol can produce a small, predominantly fat gain at the cost of thrombosis, edema and increased mortality.
highlightAliases.new: The book cites the Beers Criteria recommendation to avoid megestrol and cyproheptadine in older adults; megestrol can produce a small, predominantly fat gain at the cost of thrombosis, edema and increased mortality.
